terms.comment: Cicero’s word for the lasting distress of mind that his philosophy treats as an illness of the soul (Tusc. 3–4), and the nearest classical word for depression; it is also grief and sorrow in general. Of the body, illness, only after Augustus (Lewis & Short).
Cicero’s contrast to effūsiō animī in joy: the shrinking of the mind in pain.
Literally having black bile; Cicero cites it from Aristotle.

phrases.latin: sed cum mē aegritūdō nōn sōlum somnō prīvāret vērum nē vigilāre quidem sine summō dolōre paterētur
phrases.english: but since my distress not only robbed me of sleep but would not even let me be awake without the greatest pain

phrases.latin: Aristotelēs quidem ait omnēs ingeniōsōs melancholicōs esse
phrases.english: Aristotle indeed says that all men of genius are melancholic
